cards.text: Paul is writing a letter to God's people in Rome. He just finished telling them to overcome evil with good. Now he turns to the governing authorities, the people in charge.

cards.question: Paul says only the believers in Rome must submit to the governing authorities.
Why does Paul say everyone must submit to the governing authorities?

answers.text: There is no authority except from God
Rulers always know what is best
The law of Moses commands it

cards.text: Paul says, "The authorities that exist have been appointed by God." So whoever resists authority is opposing what God has set in place. The dead batteries I shared that drawer with tried to take charge once. Said they had the power. Friend, they did NOT have the power.

cards.question: Paul says whoever resists authority is opposing what God has set in place, and will bring ___ on themselves.

cards.text: Next, Paul talks about rulers, and who ought to be nervous around them. A police car pulls up behind me in traffic and I start SWEATING. I don't even drive. I'm a cookie stamper.

cards.question: Paul says rulers are a terror to good conduct.
Paul asks if you want to be unafraid of the one in authority. What does he tell you to do?
Paul says the one in authority is God's ___ for your good.

cards.text: But then Paul flips it. If you do wrong, he says, be afraid.

cards.question: If you do wrong, Paul says to be afraid of the one in authority, because he does not carry the ___ in vain.

cards.text: Paul says, "He is God’s servant, an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer." Then Paul gets to his "therefore."

cards.question: Paul says it's necessary to submit to authority, not only to avoid punishment. What's the other reason?
Paul says this is also why you pay something. What is it?

cards.text: Paul says the authorities are God's servants, who devote themselves to their work. Friend, I never paid a tax in my life. Years in a junk drawer, and the tax man never found me. Nobody found me. That was the whole problem.

cards.question: Paul says to pay everyone what you owe. Besides taxes and revenue, he says to pay ___ and ___ to whom they're due.

cards.text: Paul's whole list: "taxes to whom taxes are due, revenue to whom revenue is due, respect to whom respect is due, honor to whom honor is due." That's a long bill, friend. And half of it you can't pay with money.

findings.problem: The card states a fact from outside the passage (Paul just told them to overcome evil with good, Romans 12:21) without its reference. The card's citation also stops at Romans 13:1.

rule.text: **References.** Every Bible fact he states carries its reference.

findings.problem: The story card runs five sentences: the quote, the consequence and a three-sentence joke.

rule.text: **Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.**

findings.problem: The battery joke is about grabbing power the batteries don't have. The verses are about resisting the authority God has set in place. The comparison's action doesn't match the fact's action.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The story card runs three sentences.

rule.text: **Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.**

findings.problem: The rest of Romans 13:3, 'you will have his approval', is never told or asked anywhere in the stop. That leaves a gap in Paul's reasoning.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: The card tells Paul getting to his 'therefore', which is from Romans 13:5. The card only cites Romans 13:4.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'To earn a good name' is close to Romans 13:3, where doing right earns the ruler's approval. A baker could argue for it.

rule.text: Each wrong answer must be false anywhere in the passage, not just at that moment.

findings.problem: The question says 'this is also why you pay something'. 'This' points back to a reason on an earlier card the baker can no longer see.

rule.text: **Always give context in the question.** The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: The story card runs five sentences.

rule.text: **Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.**

findings.problem: The two blanks make the baker guess the next words of Paul's list (respect, honor). No earlier card sets up a way to reason them out over 'prayers' or 'offerings'.

rule.text: **Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.**

findings.problem: The story card runs three sentences.

rule.text: **Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.**

findings.problem: The question types run in a repeating pattern: true or false, multiple choice, fill in the blank, then true or false, multiple choice, fill in the blank (cards 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9).

rule.text: **No formula.** Which question type comes next, the order the types come in and where a blank falls are chosen naturally for each card. They never follow a pattern.
